subject: Pathology
vignette: A 34-year-old man is seen 5 days after a clean 4 cm laceration was sutured. The wound is sealed, granulation tissue fills the defect, and new capillaries are visible at the wound base. A surgical resident describes the phases of wound healing.
question: Which of the following cell types is the predominant effector of collagen deposition at this stage of healing?

options.text: Neutrophils
Platelets
Erythrocytes
Mast cells
Fibroblasts and myofibroblasts

explanation_correct: The proliferative phase, lasting from day 3 to weeks after the wound, is driven by fibroblasts, myofibroblasts, endothelial cells, keratinocytes, and macrophages. Its features are deposition of granulation tissue and type III collagen, angiogenesis, epithelial proliferation, dissolution of the clot, and wound contraction mediated by myofibroblasts. Platelets, neutrophils, and macrophages dominate the earlier inflammatory phase up to 3 days, and fibroblasts alone later perform remodeling.

explanation_incorrect.A: Neutrophils belong to the inflammatory phase of the first 3 days, clearing debris and migrating into the tissue before collagen is laid down.
explanation_incorrect.B: Platelets dominate the earliest clot formation step of the inflammatory phase rather than collagen synthesis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Erythrocytes are red blood cells trapped in the wound and play no role in granulation tissue formation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Mast cells contribute vasoactive mediators to inflammation and are not the effector cells of collagen deposition.

educationalObjective: In the proliferative phase of wound healing, fibroblasts and myofibroblasts deposit type III collagen and contract the wound.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 60-year-old woman has a healing abdominal wound that appears weak and slow to mature 3 weeks after surgery. She has a history of poor diet and chronic alcoholism, and her diet is deficient in a vitamin required for hydroxylation of proline in collagen.
question: Which of the following best explains her impaired wound healing?

options.text: Deficiency of vitamin D prevents cross-linking of collagen fibrils
Deficiency of vitamin A prevents angiogenesis in granulation tissue
Deficiency of vitamin K prevents synthesis of type III collagen
Deficiency of vitamin C delays the second and proliferative phase of wound healing
Deficiency of zinc accelerates wound contraction and improves tensile strength

explanation_correct: The text states that the delayed second phase of wound healing occurs in vitamin C and copper deficiency, so a scorbutic diet slows granulation tissue formation and collagen deposition during the proliferative phase. The timing matters, because vitamin C is a cofactor for collagen hydroxylation and its absence limits the type III collagen that must be laid down from day 3 onward. Zinc deficiency is a separate listed cause of delayed wound healing that operates in the remodeling phase through collagenase activity.

explanation_incorrect.A: Vitamin D is not required for collagen cross-linking; the text names vitamin C and copper as the deficiencies that delay the second phase.
explanation_incorrect.B: Angiogenesis in granulation tissue is stimulated by vascular endothelial growth factor and fibroblast growth factor rather than being a vitamin A dependent step.
explanation_incorrect.C: Vitamin K is a cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors, and the text attributes collagen maturation to zinc-dependent collagenases instead.
explanation_incorrect.E: Zinc deficiency delays wound healing rather than accelerating contraction and improving tensile strength.

educationalObjective: Vitamin C and copper deficiency delay the proliferative phase of wound healing, while zinc deficiency delays remodeling.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 46-year-old man returns 4 months after an appendectomy with a well-healed surgical scar. The wound is flat and nonpainful, and the surgeon notes that the scar has now separated fully from the underlying fascia. Biopsy shows abundant new connective tissue with few residual cells.
question: Which of the following best describes the collagen changes that have occurred in this scar?

options.text: Type III collagen has been replaced by type I collagen, increasing tensile strength
Type I collagen has been replaced by type III collagen, weakening the tissue
Collagen deposition has increased without any change in collagen type
Type IV collagen has been deposited by endothelial cells in the scar
No collagen remodeling occurs after 3 months because healing has finished

explanation_correct: The remodeling phase extends from 1 week to 6 or more months after the wound, and during it type III collagen is replaced by type I collagen, which increases the tensile strength of the tissue. Collagenases that require zinc to function break down the type III collagen during this exchange, which is why zinc deficiency delays wound healing. Scar tissue regains roughly 70 to 80 percent of tensile strength at 3 months, with little additional strength gained thereafter.

explanation_incorrect.B: The replacement occurs in the opposite direction; type III is the immature provisional collagen of granulation tissue and is progressively exchanged for type I.
explanation_incorrect.C: The defining event of remodeling is the change in collagen type as well as the reorganization of collagen fibers.
explanation_incorrect.D: Type IV collagen belongs to basement membranes supporting endothelial cells, not to the fibrous scar matrix.
explanation_incorrect.E: Remodeling continues for 6 or more months, and the collagen type switch happens during this prolonged phase.

educationalObjective: During remodeling, type III collagen is replaced by type I collagen, increasing tensile strength, and this requires zinc-dependent collagenases.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 58-year-old woman with a chronic venous ulcer undergoes debridement. The surgeon describes the mediators that will orchestrate granulation tissue formation, angiogenesis, and the eventual fibrous scar.
question: Which of the following mediator pairs is most directly responsible for angiogenesis and fibrosis during this repair process?

options.text: Interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor for angiogenesis, with interferon gamma for fibrosis
Histamine and prostaglandin E2 for angiogenesis, with bradykinin for fibrosis
C3a and C5a for angiogenesis, with C-reactive protein for fibrosis
Vascular endothelial growth factor and fibroblast growth factor for angiogenesis, with transforming growth factor beta for fibrosis
Myeloperoxidase and NADPH oxidase for angiogenesis, with haptoglobin for fibrosis

explanation_correct: The tissue mediators of wound healing listed in the text include vascular endothelial growth factor and fibroblast growth factor, both of which stimulate angiogenesis, and transforming growth factor beta, which promotes both angiogenesis and fibrosis. In addition, platelet-derived growth factor induces vascular remodeling and stimulates fibroblast growth for collagen synthesis, while metalloproteinases remodel the matrix and epidermal growth factor stimulates cell growth through tyrosine kinases such as EGFR/ErbB1. Excess TGF-beta is associated with aberrant scarring such as hypertrophic and keloid scars.

explanation_incorrect.A: IL-1 and TNF are pyrogenic inflammatory cytokines, and interferon gamma activates macrophages for killing rather than driving fibrosis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Histamine and prostaglandin E2 mediate the vascular signs of acute inflammation, and bradykinin mediates pain rather than fibrous repair.
explanation_incorrect.C: C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins and chemoattractants, and C-reactive protein is an acute-phase opsonin, none of which stimulate angiogenesis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Myeloperoxidase and NADPH oxidase generate microbicidal oxidants, and haptoglobin binds extracellular hemoglobin to limit oxidative stress.

educationalObjective: VEGF and FGF stimulate angiogenesis while TGF-beta drives angiogenesis and fibrosis, and excess TGF-beta produces aberrant scars.
